You have a close relationship with a vendor who privately tells you that they have identified a vulnerability in their web application that can be exploited through an XSS attack. The application runs on servers both in the cloud and on-premises. Before the CVE is released, you want to search your environment for signs that the vulnerability has been exploited. What should you do?

options.text: Create a YARA-L 2.0 rule to detect a time-ordered series of events where an external inbound connection to a server was followed by a process on the server that spawned subprocesses previously not seen in the environment.

Create a YARA-L 2.0 rule to detect high-prevalence binaries on your web server architecture communicating with known command and control (C2) nodes. Review inbound traffic from those C2 domains that have only started appearing recently.
Ask the Gemini Agent in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to search for the latest vulnerabilities in the environment.
Activate a new Web Security Scanner scan in Security Command Center (SCC), and look for findings related to XSS.

questions.explanation:
A multi-event YARA-L 2.0 rule can correlate an external inbound connection to a server with unusual process and subprocess activity on that same server within a defined time window, providing behavior-based detection of possible exploitation before public CVE-based indicators exist. Google Security Operations supports YARA-L multi-event correlation over temporal windows. Web Security Scanner detects web-application vulnerabilities in supported Google Cloud resources, but it does not hunt for exploitation activity across both cloud and on-premises servers.

**Learn more:** [YARA-L match section syntax](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/yara-l/match-syntax) · [Overview of Web Security Scanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-web-security-scanner-overview?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is a Google Security Operations (SecOps) customer and uses Google Threat Intelligence to identify cyber threats within its threat profile. You believe that your organization may have been targeted by a cybercrime group. You need to determine whether your organization has been the victim of an attack. What should you do?

options.text: Implement monitors in the Digital Threat Monitoring feature to identify new compromised credentials, dark web mentions, or data leaks.

In the Reports & Analysis feature, extract the IOCs from the recent reports, and implement detection rules and lists in Google SecOps to identify whether they are present in your organization's environment.

Review the Threat Landscape feature to identify threat groups that are active in your industry, research their known MITRE ATT&CK tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and implement detection rules in Google SecOps.
In the Vulnerability Intelligence feature, identify new high and critical vulnerabilities in products or technologies that your organization uses so they can be patched.

questions.explanation:
Matching indicators of compromise (IoCs) from recent threat reports against the organization’s ingested security telemetry provides direct evidence of whether the suspected threat actor’s infrastructure, malware, or other known indicators are present in the environment. Google SecOps continuously evaluates telemetry against threat-intelligence IoCs and generates alerts when matches are found.

**Learn more:** [Applied Threat Intelligence overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/applied-threat-intel-overview) · [View IoCs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-view-ioc-page?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a security analyst at an organization using Google Security Operations (SecOps). Google SecOps generated a medium-severity **Unusual Cloud Storage Access - High Volume Download** alert for [email protected] from the `internal-project-code-repository` bucket. This senior developer has legitimate access within your organization, but their download volume is unusually high and takes place outside working hours. You need to investigate this alert. What should you do first?

options.text: Run a Google SecOps SOAR playbook to suspend user1's bucket access, and review their user timeline.
Enrich the bucket entity with sensitivity labels and access control list (ACL) data.
Create a default detection rule in Google SecOps to monitor future high-volume downloads from the bucket, and add user1 to a high-risk watchlist.
Review user1's timeline in Google SecOps, focusing on network events and resource access immediately preceding the download anomaly.

questions.explanation:
An anomalous download by a user with legitimate access should initially be triaged by correlating the user’s activity around the event. Examining network events and resource-access activity immediately before the download can establish whether the behavior is consistent with normal work or indicates account compromise or data exfiltration. Google SecOps investigation guidance recommends pivoting to an entity’s timeline to review historical context and correlated events before follow-up actions.

**Learn more:** [Investigate alerts and entity context | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/Investigate-alert-entity-context?hl=en) · [Filter data in User view | Google Security Operations](https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/filter-data-user-view)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are investigating whether an advanced persistent threat (APT) actor has been operating undetected in your organization's environment. You have received threat intelligence that includes:  
  
- A SHA256 hash for a malicious DLL  
- A known command and control (C2) domain  
- A behavior pattern in which `rundll32.exe` spawns `powershell.exe` with obfuscated arguments  
  
Your Google Security Operations (SecOps) instance contains logs from EDR, DNS, and Windows Sysmon. However, you recently discovered that process hashes are not captured reliably across all endpoints because the Sysmon configuration is inconsistent. You need to use Google SecOps to develop a detection mechanism that identifies the related activities. What should you do?

options.text: Write a multi-event YARA-L detection rule that correlates the process relationship and hash, and run a retrohunt based on this rule.
Build a reference list that contains the hash and domain, and link the list to a high-frequency rule for near real-time alerting.
Create a single-event YARA-L detection rule based on the file hash, and run the rule against historical and incoming telemetry to detect the DLL execution.
Use Google SecOps search to identify recent uses of rundll32.exe, and tag affected assets for watchlisting.

questions.explanation:
A multi-event YARA-L rule can correlate the suspicious `rundll32.exe` to obfuscated `powershell.exe` process relationship with related DNS activity to the known C2 domain, using the DLL hash as corroborating evidence when present. This behavioral, cross-source approach remains effective when hash collection is incomplete. A retrohunt applies the rule to retained telemetry to identify earlier, previously undetected activity; a hash-only rule would miss endpoints that did not record process hashes.

**Learn more:** [Detection rules overview | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/default-rules) · [Run a rule against historical data | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization intends to ingest logs from an on-premises MySQL database as a new log source in its Google Security Operations (SecOps) instance. You need to create a solution that minimizes effort. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a third-party API feed in Google SecOps.
Configure direct ingestion from your Google Cloud organization.
Configure and deploy a Google SecOps forwarder.
Configure and deploy a Bindplane collection agent.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps supports MySQL log collection through the Bindplane agent, which is designed to collect logs from on-premises servers. Direct ingestion is intended for Google Cloud logs, while third-party API feeds address API or cloud-to-cloud integrations; the legacy forwarder is deprecated.

**Learn more:** [Collect MySQL logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/mysql) · [Ingestion methods and data types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/data-types)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying Google Security Operations (SecOps) for your organization. The organization has its own threat-intelligence feed, which was ingested into Google SecOps through a native Malware Information Sharing Platform (MISP) integration. You are developing the following detection rule to use command-and-control (C2) indicators ingested into the entity graph.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783903612182-arl1r5gs.png)  
  
What code should you add to the detection rule to filter for domain IOCs?

options.text: $ioc.graph.metadata.entity_type =
$ioc.graph.metadata.entity_type =
$ioc.graph.metadata.entity_type =
$ioc.graph.metadata.entity_type =

questions.explanation:
Customer-provided IOC feeds ingested into the Google SecOps entity graph are labeled with `source_type = "ENTITY_CONTEXT"`. Filtering on `entity_type = "DOMAIN_NAME"` limits the joined indicators to domains, so the required filter is the `DOMAIN_NAME` and `ENTITY_CONTEXT` combination.

**Learn more:** [Manage alerts and IOC matches](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/alerts-iocs?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Google Security Operations (SecOps) to investigate suspicious activity associated with a specific user. You want to identify every asset the user interacted with during the past seven days to assess the potential impact. You need to understand the user's relationships to endpoints, service accounts, and cloud resources. How should you identify user-to-asset relationships in Google SecOps?

options.text: Use the Raw Log Scan view to group events by asset ID.
Query for hostnames in UDM Search and filter the results by user.
Generate an ingestion report to identify sources where the user appeared in the last seven days.
Run a retrohunt to find rule matches triggered by the user.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps UDM Search supports queries on user fields and returns normalized events and entity details for the selected time range. Its user entity view includes associated entities, including assets the user accessed, so filtering UDM Search results for the user and examining hostname or asset fields identifies user-to-asset relationships. Raw-log scans, ingestion reports, and retrohunts do not provide this relationship-focused entity investigation.

**Learn more:** [Investigate an entity using UDM search](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/udm-search-investigate-entity) · [Understand search](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/udm-search)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Security Command Center (SCC) and Google Security Operations (SecOps). Last week, an attacker tried to establish persistence by creating a key for an unused service account.  
  
You need to verify that alerts are received when keys are created for unused service accounts and that newly created keys are automatically deleted. You want to minimize the required manual effort. What should you do?

options.text: Generate a YARA-L rule in Google SecOps that detects when a service account key is created. Using the built-in IDE, create a custom action in Google SecOps SOAR that deletes the service account key.

Use the Initial Access: Dormant Service Account Key Created finding from SCC, and ingest this finding into Google SecOps. Create a custom action in Google SecOps SOAR that is triggered on this finding. Use the built-in IDE to build code to delete the service account key.
Configure a Cloud Logging sink to write logs to a Pub/Sub topic that filters for the methodName:

Use the Initial Access: Dormant Service Account Key Created finding from SCC, and write this finding to a Pub/Sub topic. Create a Cloud Run function that subscribes to the Pub/Sub topic and deletes the service account key.

questions.explanation:
Security Command Center's `Initial Access: Dormant Service Account Key Created` finding is generated when a user-managed key is created for a service account inactive for more than 180 days. Sending that specific finding to Google SecOps supplies targeted alerting, while a Google SecOps SOAR custom action can be invoked through automation to delete the newly created service-account key. This uses the built-in dormant-account detection instead of implementing separate log filtering and Cloud Run remediation infrastructure.

You are developing a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR playbook that uses the VirusTotal v3 integration to look up a URL reported by a threat hunter in an email. You need to use the results to make an initial recommendation about the URL's maliciousness and set the alert severity based on the output. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a widget that translates the JSON output to a severity score.
Use the number of detections from the response JSON in a conditional statement to set the severity.
Verify that the response is accurate by manually checking the URL in VirusTotal
Pass the response back to the SIEM.
Use a conditional statement to determine whether to treat the URL as suspicious or benign.

questions.explanation:
VirusTotal URL reputation results can be evaluated through playbook condition branches. The detection count in the response JSON provides a programmable signal for assigning severity, while a conditional branch can classify the URL for preliminary handling as suspicious or benign. Google Security Operations documents configuring condition branches to evaluate a reputation scan's JSON result and branching based on malicious versus clean or unknown results.

**Learn more:** [Explore playbook use cases](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/playbooks-use-cases)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a SOC manager overseeing implementation of your existing incident response plan (IRP) in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You need to record time-duration data for every case stage. You want the solution to require minimal maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a detection rule in SIEM Rules & Detections to include logic to capture the event fields for each case with the relevant stage metrics.
Write a job in the IDE that runs frequently to check the progress of each case and updates the notes with timestamps to reflect when these changes were identified.
Configure Case Stages in the Google SecOps SOAR settings, and use the Change Case Stage action in your playbooks that captures time metrics when the stage changes.
Create a Google SecOps SOAR dashboard that displays specific actions that have been run, identifies which stage a case is in, and calculates the time elapsed since the start of the case.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps SOAR supports configurable case stages and automated case-stage transitions through the `Change Case Stage` playbook action. Its reporting capabilities calculate the average handling time spent in each stage, from the start of that stage until the case moves to another stage or closes. This uses platform-native stage history and avoids maintaining custom polling, timestamp notes, or detection-rule logic.

**Learn more:** [Manage case stages | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/investigate/working-with-cases/adddelete-case-stages-admin) · [Work with SOAR reports | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/monitor-and-report/soar-reports/using-looker-explores-in-soar-reports)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company's SOC recently handled a ransomware incident that started with the execution of a malicious document. EDR tools contained the initial infection. However, several privileged service accounts continued to show anomalous activity, including credential dumping and scheduled-task creation. You need to design an automated playbook in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR to reduce dwell time and speed containment for similar future attacks. Which action should you include in your Google SecOps SOAR playbook to support containment and escalation?

options.text: Configure a step that revokes OAuth tokens and suspends sessions for high-privilege accounts based on entity risk.
Add an approval step that requires an analyst to validate the alert before executing a containment action.
Create an external API call to VirusTotal to submit hashes from forensic artifacts.
Add a YARA-L rule that sends an alert when a document is executed using a scripting engine such as wscript.exe.

questions.explanation:
Revoking OAuth tokens and suspending active sessions for high-privilege accounts whose entity risk is elevated immediately limits continued use of compromised credentials and reduces the opportunity for persistence or lateral movement. Google SecOps SOAR playbooks support automated response actions and conditional flows; enrichment, alert-only detection, and a manual approval gate do not provide the same immediate containment.

**Learn more:** [Google Security Operations SOAR overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/overview-and-introduction/soar-overview) · [Playbook and automation overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/whats-on-the-playbooks-screen)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying Google Security Operations (SecOps) in your organization. You find that the existing detection rules are overly noisy. Because alert volume is high, some true positives could be overlooked. You want to ingest additional context sources to lower false positives in security detections and improve the alerts’ overall positive ratio. What should you do?

options.text: Ingest high-value asset (HVA) data from your configuration management database (CMDB) system to increase the priority of the alerts based on the sensitivity of the assets found in the detection rules.
Ingest dark web forum handlers from your threat intelligence system to match dark web principals within the detection rules.
Ingest IOCs from your threat intelligence system to validate the IP addresses, domains and hashes with the detection rules.
Ingest tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) from your threat intelligence system to validate the processes and tools with the detection rules.

questions.explanation:
Indicators of compromise (IOCs) let Google Security Operations correlate observed IP addresses, domains, and file hashes with known malicious indicators from threat-intelligence feeds. This supplies direct validation context for detections, increasing confidence in alerts and reducing false-positive noise. Asset data is useful for alert prioritization, but it does not validate whether the observed activity is malicious.

**Learn more:** [Manage alerts and IOC matches | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/alerts-iocs?hl=en) · [Applied Threat Intelligence overview | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/applied-threat-intel-overview)

options.text: Enable curated detections to identify threats.
Design YARA-L detection rules based on Google SecOps Marketplace use cases.
Develop YARA-L detection rules that focus on threat intelligence.
Ingest data from a threat intelligence platform (TIP) into Google SecOps.

questions.explanation:
Google Security Operations curated detections are Google-managed, predefined threat analytics delivered as YARA-L rule sets. Enabling the applicable rule sets applies immediately actionable detection intelligence to ingested data without the time required to author custom rules or integrate a separate threat-intelligence platform.

**Learn more:** [Use curated detections to identify threats](https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/use-curated-detections)

Your company partners with an external Managed Service Provider (MSP) whose users must be able to list Security Command Center (SCC) findings by using the Google Cloud SDK. You need to configure the necessary access for the managed service provider while minimizing your involvement in managing their external user lifecycle. What should you do?

options.text: Create a user account in your Cloud Identity instance using a subdomain indicating they are external to your organization. Grant this user account the appropriate IAM role at the organization level.
Create a service account in a SCC project. Grant the MSP user permission to impersonate this account. Grant this service account the appropriate IAM role at the organization level.

Create a workload identity pool in a SCC project. Grant the MSP user the permission to impersonate a service account from this pool, and grant the service account the appropriate IAM role at the organization level.
Create a workforce identity pool and federate with the identity provider (IdP) of the managed service provider. Grant users of the MSP the appropriate IAM role at the organization level.

questions.explanation:
Workforce Identity Federation lets external workforce users, including partners and contractors, authenticate through their own identity provider and access Google Cloud through the CLI and APIs. Because identities are federated rather than created or synchronized as Cloud Identity accounts, the MSP retains responsibility for its users’ lifecycle. Granting the appropriate organization-level Security Command Center IAM role to the federated MSP principals provides the required findings-listing access.

**Learn more:** [Workforce Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workforce-identity-federation) · [Configure Workforce Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/configuring-workforce-identity-federation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You notice several separate, low-severity suspicious activities linked to one internal server. You conclude that no individual event is a high-confidence IOC. You need to implement a solution that provides ongoing, heightened scrutiny of this server. What should you do?

options.text: Schedule a daily Google Security Operations (SecOps) report detailing all activity on this server.
Develop a YARA-L detection rule specific to this server.
Add the server to a Google Security Operations (SecOps) watchlist, and monitor the watchlist closely for the next few weeks.
Create a case, isolate the server from the network, and escalate the case for forensic investigation.

questions.explanation: Adding the server to a Google Security Operations watchlist enables targeted monitoring and correlation of subsequent activity involving that entity. This is appropriate when weak, individually inconclusive signals collectively justify heightened observation but do not yet warrant containment or forensic escalation.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization maintains a standard collection of Google Security Operations (SecOps) playbooks that are applied to alerts under different circumstances. One playbook uses an "All" trigger and should always apply when no other, more specific playbook has triggered. You must ensure that, when multiple triggers match, the specific playbook is attached rather than the generic "All" playbook. What should you do?

options.text: Set the priority of the
Change the
In the Outcomes section of the detection rule that is firing your alert, add a specific field to search for the specific playbook to base the trigger on.
Create a tagging rule in the Google SecOps SOAR settings, and use a tag trigger to trigger the specific playbook.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps attaches only one playbook automatically based on its priority. A fallback playbook that uses the `All` trigger should be assigned the lowest priority, priority 3, so an event-specific or product-specific playbook at a higher priority is attached whenever it matches.

**Learn more:** [Create a fallback playbook | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/create-a-catch-all-triage-playbook) · [Playbook and automation overview | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/whats-on-the-playbooks-screen)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps). You need to identify the processes and applications that occur most often across your organization’s large number of servers so that you can regularly implement baselines and exclusion lists. You want to take the most efficient approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use the UDM lookup feature to identify relevant process-related UDM fields and values.
Run a UDM search, and review aggregations for relevant process-related UDM fields.
Review the Google SecOps SIEM Rules & Detections, and identify the most common processes appearing in alerts that are marked as false positives.
Generate a Google SecOps SIEM dashboard based on relevant UDM fields, such as processes, that provides the counts for process names and files.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps UDM Search aggregations show the event count for each UDM-field value and order the values from highest to lowest count. Reviewing aggregations for process-related UDM fields therefore directly reveals the processes and applications occurring most frequently, supporting baseline and exclusion-list creation.

**Learn more:** [Understand search | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/udm-search)

",["$","$L57",null,{"choices":{"A":"Set the priority of the "All" playbook to a higher value than the priority of the specific playbook to ensure the "All" trigger is evaluated after the previous priorities.","B":"Change the "All" trigger to be more precise so that it doesn't trigger when the other playbook is needed.","C":"In the Outcomes section of the detection rule that is firing your alert, add a specific field to search for the specific playbook to base the trigger on.","D":"Create a tagging rule in the Google SecOps SOAR settings, and use a tag trigger to trigger the specific playbook."},"correctAnswer":"A","explanation":"Google SecOps attaches only one playbook automatically based on its priority. Your company recently began importing JSON logs from a third-party system into Google Security Operations (SecOps). You discovered that some fields are absent and want to parse them into UDM fields as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Configure auto extraction to add the additional fields.
Create parser extensions using the no-code approach.
Create parser extensions using the code snippet approach.
Submit a parser improvement request to Cloud Customer Care.

questions.explanation:
For JSON logs, a no-code parser extension can map raw JSON field paths directly to destination UDM fields without writing parser code. Auto extraction stores values in the `extracted` map-type field rather than normalizing them into selected UDM fields. [Google Security Operations parser extensions documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/using-parser-extensions)

**Learn more:** [Develop parser extensions | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/using-parser-extensions) · [Auto-extraction overview | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/auto-extraction)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is moving to a multi-cloud environment. You need to set up comprehensive threat monitoring with Google Security Operations (SecOps) and want to begin identifying threats as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Use Gemini to generate YARA-L rules for multi-cloud use cases.
Use curated detections from the Cloud Threats category to monitor your cloud environment.
Use curated detections for Applied Threat Intelligence to monitor your company's cloud environment.
Ask Cloud Customer Care to provide a set of rules recommended by Google to monitor your company's cloud environment.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Threats category provides Google-managed curated detections for Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure data. These prebuilt rule sets can be enabled to evaluate incoming cloud telemetry and produce detections and alerts, providing broad multi-cloud threat coverage without first developing custom rules.

**Learn more:** [Cloud threats | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/cloud-threats-category) · [Use curated detections to identify threats | Google Security Operations](https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/use-curated-detections)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage threat intelligence and IOC lists for your organization. You have compiled IOCs from recent incidents and want to share them quickly and efficiently with other teams for collaboration and integration into their operational processes. What should you do?

options.text: Create a list in Google Security Operations (SecOps), and grant the required access to the other teams.
Export the IOCs from Google Threat Intelligence in CSV or JSON format, and email the file to the other teams.
Add the IOCs to a collection in Google Threat Intelligence, and share the collection with the other teams.
Create a new threat graph in Google Threat Intelligence, and share the graph with the other teams.

questions.explanation:
Google Threat Intelligence IoC Collections are live reports that group file hashes, URLs, domains, and IP addresses, and they can be shared with other users. This enables teams to collaborate on the same IOC set while retaining continuously updated threat-intelligence analysis and context, supporting operational use beyond a static emailed export.

**Learn more:** [IoC Collections | Google Threat Intelligence Documentation](https://gtidocs.virustotal.com/docs/ioc-collections)

questions.question: Your organization is a Google Security Operations (SecOps) customer that monitors critical assets through a SIEM dashboard. You need to dynamically monitor those assets using a specific asset tag. What should you do?

options.text: Ask Cloud Customer Care to add a custom filter to the dashboard.
Add a custom filter to the dashboard.
Copy an existing dashboard and add a custom filter.
Export the dashboard configuration to a file, modify the file to add a custom filter, and import the file into Google SecOps.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps supports adding dashboard-level custom filters to refine the data shown in applicable charts. Configuring a filter for the relevant asset-tag field lets the dashboard dynamically display assets matching that tag.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure dashboard filters | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/native-dashboards-filters)

questions.question: Your organization is a Google Security Operations (SecOps) customer that monitors critical assets through a SIEM dashboard. You need to dynamically monitor those assets using a specific asset tag. What should you do?

options.text: Perform a UDM search across the logs for domains with geolocations that were first seen in the last 30 days.
Perform a UDM search across the logs for domains with low prevalence that were first seen in the last 30 days.
Perform a raw log search across the logs for domains with low prevalence that were first seen in the last 30 days.
Identify the domains with the higher normalized risk in Risk Analytics. Drill down into those entities to determine their prevalence and if they were first seen in the last 30 days.

Navigate to the IOC Matches page and filter based on domain type over the last 30 days. Look for the first seen and last seen timestamps for the reported domains. Investigate these domains using the IOC drilldown link.

questions.explanation:
Domain prevalence and first-seen metadata are derived context available through normalized UDM/entity-context searches, so searching for low-prevalence domains first observed within the last 30 days targets the stated anomaly criteria. Applied Threat Intelligence produces IOC matches and supports investigating matched domain IOCs from the IOC Matches page, including first-seen and last-seen details and IOC drilldown.

**Learn more:** [Investigate an entity using UDM search](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/udm-search-investigate-entity) · [Entity Context Graph overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/entity-graph)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is a Google Security Operations (SecOps) customer. The compliance team requires a weekly export of case resolutions and SLA metrics for high- and critical-severity cases from the past week. The compliance team's post-processing scripts require the data to be formatted as tabular CSV files, zipped, and delivered to their email each Monday morning. What should you do?

options.text: Generate a report in SOAR Reports, and schedule delivery of the report.
Use statistics in search, and configure a Google SecOps SOAR job to format and send the report.
Build an Advanced Report in SOAR Reports, and schedule delivery of the report.
Build a detection rule with outcomes, and configure a Google SecOps SOAR job to format and send the report.

questions.explanation:
SOAR Reports can be scheduled, but their documented export formats are PDF and Word rather than CSV. Search statistics can produce filtered, tabular case data, and a scheduled Google SecOps SOAR job can automate the required CSV formatting, ZIP packaging, and Monday email delivery. Advanced SOAR reporting supports analysis of case priority, closure, and SLA fields, but the required custom packaging and delivery workflow calls for a job.

**Learn more:** [Explore legacy SOAR reports](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/monitor-and-report/soar-reports/understanding-reports?hl=en) · [Work with SOAR reports](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/monitor-and-report/soar-reports/using-looker-explores-in-soar-reports)

questions.question:
You are planning log onboarding for a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM deployment in a cloud-heavy enterprise environment. The detection engineering team requests log sources that provide visibility into:  
  
- User identity behavior  
- Lateral movement  
- Privilege-escalation attempts  
  
You need to decide which telemetry sources to ingest first. Which log source should you prioritize?

options.text: Cloud access security broker (CASB) logs
EDR logs
IAM logs
Network firewall logs

questions.explanation: IAM logs record authentication, authorization, role-assumption, policy-change, and permission-change activity. This telemetry is foundational for detecting anomalous identity behavior, cloud lateral movement through credential or role use, and privilege-escalation attempts.

questions.question:
You are planning log onboarding for a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM deployment in a cloud-heavy enterprise environment. The detection engineering team requests log sources that provide visibility into:  
  
- User identity behavior  
- Lateral movement  
- Privilege-escalation attempts  
  
You need to decide which telemetry sources to ingest first. Which log source should you prioritize?

options.text: Enable VM Manager across your projects, and allow VM Manager to write findings to SCCE.
Enable Virtual Machine Threat Detection in SCCE, and allow it to generate findings.
Set up Google Open Source Vulnerability (OSV)-Scanner to scan all Compute Engine VMs. Configure a Google Security Operations (SecOps) forwarder to write logs to your Google SecOps instance.
Create a custom Security Health Analytics (SHA) scanner to check the sourceImage of the compute disk. Check for matches in a vulnerability database.

questions.explanation:
VM Manager uses OS inventory to identify CVEs affecting installed operating-system packages on supported Compute Engine VMs. When integrated with organization-level Security Command Center Enterprise, it automatically sends high- and critical-severity OS vulnerability findings to Security Command Center, providing centralized, managed visibility across projects. Virtual Machine Threat Detection is for detecting threats such as malware, rootkits, and cryptomining rather than identifying OS package CVEs.

**Learn more:** [Security Command Center detection services: VM Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-security-sources) · [VM Manager OS inventory management](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/vm-manager/docs/os-inventory/os-inventory-management)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team performs threat hunting for a large multinational corporation. You subscribe to third-party threat intelligence feeds and want to implement a solution that continuously compares DNS calls on endpoints with those feeds. What should you do?

options.text: Use custom modules in Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center (SCC) to correlate feed data with Google Cloud logs.
Push endpoint logs to BigQuery and use scripts to compare entries to Google Threat intelligence by using a Google Threat Intelligence API key.
Create a YARA-L rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to track matches between the ingested EDR log entries and the entity graph.
Create a YARA-L rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to track matches between the ingested EDR log entries and the VirusTotal table in the entity graph.

questions.explanation:
Google Security Operations can ingest proprietary or third-party threat-intelligence feeds as entity context and correlate them with normalized security events. A YARA-L detection rule can join ingested EDR DNS events to domain-name indicators in the Entity Context Graph, enabling continuous matching against the subscribed feeds. The VirusTotal table represents only a specific Google-provided intelligence source, not the organization’s third-party feeds.

**Learn more:** [Manage alerts and IOC matches](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/alerts-iocs) · [Entity Context Graph overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/entity-graph?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR integration with Security Command Center (SCC) uses a service account that currently has read access to findings at the organization level. Google SecOps SOAR can successfully read SCC finding data, but actions that attempt to update finding states consistently fail with a permission-denied error. You need to fix this error while adhering to the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the service account the roles/securitycenter.findingsBulkMuteEditor IAM role at the organization level.
Grant the service account the roles/securitycenter.findingsEditor IAM role at the organization level.
Grant the service account the roles/iam.serviceAccountUser IAM role to itself.
Regenerate the service account key, and update the credentials in Google SecOps SOAR.

questions.explanation:
The Security Center Findings Editor role (`roles/securitycenter.findingsEditor`) grants `securitycenter.findings.setState`, which authorizes updates to SCC finding states. Assigning it at the organization level covers the organization-level findings being managed.

**Learn more:** [Security Command Center roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/securitycenter) · [Managing findings using the Security Command Center API](https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-create-manage-findings)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently joined a company that uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) with Applied Threat Intelligence enabled. A recent red team exercise has caused alert fatigue, and you want to spend less time sorting through noise. You need to filter out IOCs that you believe were generated by the exercise. What should you do?

options.text: Ask Gemini to provide a list of IOCs from the red team exercise.
Filter IOCs with an ingestion time that matches the time period of the red team exercise.
Navigate to the IOC Matches page. Identify and mute the IOCs from the red team exercise.
Navigate to the IOC Matches page. Review IOCs with an Indicator Confidence Score (IC-Score) label >= 80%.

questions.explanation:
Muting the specifically identified IOC matches associated with authorized red-team activity suppresses those known, non-actionable matches and reduces analyst noise. IOC ingestion time is not a reliable proxy for the time of the exercise, and an IC-Score threshold ranks threat-intelligence confidence rather than excluding the exercise-related matches.

**Learn more:** [View IoCs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-view-ioc-page?hl=en) · [Google Security Operations SIEM release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/release-notes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has recently seen an increase in security incidents. You need to build a near-real-time visualization of activity from the last hour for users and assets that triggered alerts, grouped by the highest risk scores. What should you do?

options.text: Navigate to the Alerts & IOCs panel in Google Security Operations (SecOps). Set the showing time to the last hour, and sort by risk score.
Create a dashboard to display all alerts from the last hour, broken down by entity type and sorted by risk score.
Navigate to the Risk Analytics dashboard in Google Security Operations (SecOps). Sort the entities by normalized change.
Create a report using the events table in the BigQuery export that shows all alerts over the last hour broken out by entity type and ordered by risk score.

questions.explanation:
A Google Security Operations dashboard can visualize alerts for a selected one-hour time range, break the results down by entity type, and prioritize them by risk score. This provides an operational view of the users and assets associated with the highest-risk recent alerts. Risk Analytics is limited to 24-hour or 7-day risk-calculation windows, so it does not meet a last-hour requirement.

**Learn more:** [SIEM dashboard overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/dashboards-overview) · [Analyze risks using the dashboard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/risk-analytics-dashboard)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is performing a penetration test. The CISO has asked you to establish a real-time way to track cases originating from the penetration test and to clearly distinguish them from other security incidents. You need to recommend the most effective and efficient approach to accomplish this in Google Security Operations (SecOps). What should you do?

options.text: Implement case tagging within Google SecOps and apply a unique tag (e.g., PenTest) to all cases related to the penetration test entities. Use this tag for filtering and monitoring.
Create a dashboard that is connected to the Google SecOps data lake. Use pre-built templates to visualize case status based on the penetration testing IP address range.
Create a custom Google SecOps SOAR playbook that automatically extracts case metadata, including key findings and risk scores, and sends an email summary to the CISO.

Configure a custom alert rule that triggers a high-severity alert for all activity originating from the penetration testing team's source IP addresses and sends a notification for potential critical vulnerabilities. Verify that these alerts are immediately visible in the alert queue.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps case tags classify and organize cases, and case-queue filters support filtering by tags. Assigning a unique tag such as `PenTest` to cases associated with penetration-testing entities makes those cases immediately distinguishable and readily monitorable while preserving separation from ordinary security incidents.

**Learn more:** [Manage case and alert tags](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/investigate/working-with-cases/define-tags-in-cases-admin) · [Filter case and alert data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/investigate/working-with-cases/apply-and-save-filters)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A Google Security Operations (SecOps) detection rule is producing frequent false-positive alerts. The rule was created to detect suspicious Cloud Storage enumeration by alerting whenever the `storage.objects.list` API operation is invoked through the `api.operation` UDM field. However, a legitimate backup automation tool uses the same API, which causes the rule to fire unnecessarily. You need to reduce these false positives from this trusted backup tool while continuing to detect potentially malicious use. How should you change the rule to improve its accuracy?

options.text: Add principal.user.email !=
Replace api.operation with api.service_name =
Convert the rule into a multi-event rule that looks for repeated API calls across multiple buckets.
Adjust the rule severity to LOW to deprioritize alerts from automation tools.

questions.explanation:
Excluding the known trusted automation account from the operation-based condition suppresses its expected backup activity while retaining alerts for `storage.objects.list` calls made by every other principal. Cloud Audit Logs map the authenticated principal email into a principal user email UDM field, so an actor-specific exclusion is an appropriate way to tune a false-positive-prone detection.

**Learn more:** [Collect Google Cloud Audit Logs](https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/cloud-audit) · [UDM field dictionary reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reference/udm-field-list)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s analyst team uses a playbook to make required changes to external systems integrated with the Google Security Operations (SecOps) platform. You must automate this task so that it runs once each day at a specified time. You want the solution to minimize maintenance overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Write a custom Google SecOps SOAR job in the IDE using the code from the existing playbook actions.
Create a Google SecOps SOAR request and a playbook trigger to match the request from the user to start the playbook with the relevant actions.
Create a Cron Scheduled Connector for this use case Configure a playbook trigger to match the cases created by the connector that runs the playbook with the relevant actions.
Use a VM to host a script that runs a playbook via an API call.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps SOAR includes a Cron Scheduled Connector that triggers playbooks for a specified alert product, name, and type and supports cron expressions. Configuring the connector and a playbook trigger for its created cases reuses the existing playbook automation without requiring custom code or an externally managed VM.

**Learn more:** [Google SecOps SOAR connectors](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/marketplace/power-ups/connectors)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization recently onboarded to Google Cloud with Security Command Center Enterprise (SCCE) and is now integrating it with your organization's SOC. You want to automate the response workflow and integrate with the existing SOW ticketing system. How should you implement this capability?

options.text: Evaluate each event within the SCC console. Create a ticket for each finding in the ticketing system, and include the remediation steps.
Use the SCC notifications feed to send alerts to Pub/Sub. Ingest these feeds using the relevant SIEM connector.

Configure the SCC notifications feed to use Pub/Sub for alerts. Create a Cloud Run function to trigger when an event arrives in the topic and generate a ticket by calling the API endpoint in the SOC ticketing system.

Disable the generic posture finding playbook in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR and enable the playbook for the ticketing system. Add a step in your Google SecOps SOAR playbook to generate a ticket based on the event type.

questions.explanation:
Security Command Center Enterprise integrates ticketing through Google Security Operations SOAR playbooks. For Jira or ServiceNow, disable the default Posture Findings – Generic playbook, enable the corresponding ticketing playbook, and configure a playbook action to create tickets based on the relevant event type. The ticketing playbook also supports case-to-ticket synchronization.

**Learn more:** [Integrate Security Command Center Enterprise with ticketing systems](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/integrate-ticketing-systems) · [Playbooks overview | Security Command Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/playbooks-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying Google Security Operations (SecOps) with multiple log sources. You need to closely monitor the health of the ingestion pipeline’s forwarders and collection agents, and identify silent sources within five minutes. What should you do?

options.text: Create a notification in Cloud Monitoring using a metric-absence condition based on sample policy for each collector_id.
Create a Google SecOps SIEM dashboard to show the ingestion metrics for each log_type and collector_id.
Create an ingestion notification for health metrics in Cloud Monitoring based on the total ingested log count for each collector_id.
Create a Looker dashboard that queries the BigQuery ingestion metrics schema for each log_type and collector_id.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps silent-forwarder and silent-collection-agent monitoring is implemented through a Cloud Monitoring alert policy that groups metrics by `collector_id` and uses a metric-absence condition. Configuring the rolling window and absence duration to a combined five minutes detects collectors that stop reporting within the required interval.

**Learn more:** [Analyze ingestion with Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/ingestion-notifications-for-health-metrics?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for selecting and prioritizing potential data sources to integrate with Google Security Operations (SecOps). Your company has recently begun using several Google Cloud services to strengthen security in its Google Cloud organization. You need to identify which logs should be ingested into Google SecOps to reduce the effort needed to write detections. What should you do?

options.text: Ingest Google Cloud Armor logs by using Cloud Logging.
Deploy a Bindplane agent to ingest event logs from Compute Engine VMs that provide endpoint visibility.
Integrate Security Command Center (SCC) into Google SecOps to ingest logs originating from the Google Cloud services.
Use Google Threat Intelligence to gain insight about threat group behavior and support threat hunting activities.

questions.explanation:
Security Command Center aggregates security findings from Google Cloud services and can export those findings to Google SecOps. Google SecOps includes curated Cloud Threats rule sets that detect Security Command Center finding classes and findings from services such as Event Threat Detection and Cloud Armor, reducing the amount of custom detection logic required.

**Learn more:** [Cloud threats](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/cloud-threats-category) · [Collect Security Command Center findings](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/collect-security-command-center-findings)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are ingesting and parsing logs from an SSO provider and an on-premises appliance with Google Security Operations (SecOps). An internal process marks users as “restricted.” A restriction remains in effect for five days from the latest time the user was flagged.  
  
You need to create a rule that detects restricted users logging in to the appliance. The solution must be fast to implement and simple to maintain. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Google SecOps SOAR global context value to store a list of flagged users with their corresponding time to live values. Use a SOAR job to dynamically build and deploy a new version of the detection rule with the updated list of flagged users.
Store the identifiers of the flagged users in the detection rule logic. Actively monitor for newly flagged users, and add them to the detection rule logic.
Ingest the user flags as custom enrichment data using a feed. Use a multi-event detection rule to find logins from users flagged in the entity graph.
Store the flagged users in a data table column with their corresponding time to live values in a second column. Use row-based comparisons in your detection rule.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps can ingest user-flag data as entity context through a feed, with a validity interval representing the five-day restriction period. A multi-event detection rule can join an appliance login UDM event to that user entity context; the Detection Engine evaluates the correlation only when the login timestamp falls within the entity context record’s valid interval. This keeps the rule stable while the feed updates restricted users and their timestamps.

**Learn more:** [Overview of context-aware analytics](https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/context-aware-analytics) · [Context-enriched data in rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/use-enriched-data-in-rules)

options.text: Create a custom filter to export the folder-level Cloud NAT logs.
Create a custom filter to export the project-level Cloud NAT logs for each project in the environment folder.
Configure an aggregated log sink at the folder level, and route the Cloud NAT logs to Pub/Sub. Enable the Pub/Sub connector for Google SecOps.
Configure an aggregated log sink at the organization level, and route the Cloud NAT logs to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure the Cloud Storage connector for Google SecOps.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps direct ingestion supports Cloud NAT logs through the `log_id("compute.googleapis.com/nat_flows")` export filter. A custom export filter can be scoped to a folder, allowing the required Cloud NAT telemetry to be sent directly to SecOps without creating an intermediate Pub/Sub or Cloud Storage integration. [Ingest Google Cloud logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/ingest-gcp-logs?hl=en)

**Learn more:** [Ingest Google Cloud logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/ingest-gcp-logs?hl=en) · [Collect Cloud NAT logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/default-parsers/gcp-cloud-nat?hl=en)

You are threat hunting for an advanced threat group known for conducting targeted, novel attacks using campaign-specific infrastructure. You want to build detections from the threat group’s behaviors so that you can effectively determine whether it has attacked your organization. What should you do?

options.text: Identify exposed technologies and products used by your organization, and develop detections to search for signs of exploitation.

Find intelligence reports in Google Threat Intelligence that relate to the threat actor, identify their behavior in previous campaigns, and use the past behavior to design detections in Google Security Operations (SecOps).

Search for the threat actor in Google Threat Intelligence, export the IOCs associated with the threat actor into a Google Security Operations (SecOps) list, and develop detections that reference this list.

Search for the threat actor in Google Threat Intelligence, review the threat actor's tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), and design detections based on the TTPs in Google Security Operations (SecOps).

questions.explanation:
Campaign-specific infrastructure causes static indicators such as domains, IP addresses, and hashes to change rapidly across attacks. Threat-actor TTPs describe the more persistent behavioral patterns that can be translated into Google Security Operations detections. Google Threat Intelligence provides TTP analysis to refine detection strategies, including for proactive threat hunting.

**Learn more:** [Google Threat Intelligence — know who's targeting you](https://cloud.google.com/security/products/threat-intelligence?hl=en) · [Google Security Operations](https://cloud.google.com/security/products/security-operations)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You discovered that a server hosting an internal web application was inadvertently exposed to the internet for 48 hours. Server logging is enabled. You want to use Google Security Operations (SecOps) to perform a UDM search of the server logs to determine whether any successful exploitations occurred. Which event-field search should you use?

options.text: Perform a search for antimalware or endpoint security events by using the product_event_type UDM field.
Perform a search for sign-on activity for user accounts that are not expected on the server by using the principal.user.userid UDM field.
Perform a search for network traffic where the principal is rarely seen by using the principal.ip UDM field.
Perform a search for process launches and commands that are rarely seen by using the metadata.event_type UDM field.

questions.explanation:
Successful exploitation of a web server often produces endpoint execution evidence, including anomalous process launches and command activity. In Google SecOps UDM, `metadata.event_type` identifies the normalized type of action performed and supports `PROCESS_LAUNCH` events, making it the appropriate field for locating rare execution activity that may indicate compromise.

**Learn more:** [UDM overview | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/udm-overview) · [UDM usage guide | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/unified-data-model/udm-usage)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has onboarded a new log source from a third-party DNS filtering solution. After ingestion, you find that key UDM fields, including `network.dns.questions.name` and `metadata.product_event_type`, are absent from the parsed events in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You suspect the default parser does not fully match the source format. You need to make sure these fields are available for downstream detection rules that depend on DNS query telemetry and event categorization. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the ingestion source definition to remap raw fields directly to UDM by using the UDM sample output.
Enable asset enrichment for the log source to infer missing fields based on correlated host activity.
Use a custom parser that outputs all fields as raw JSON for detection.
Create a parser extension that maps the missing source fields to the correct UDM fields and attach it to the existing parser.

questions.explanation:
A parser extension augments the existing default parser by extracting values from the raw source logs and mapping them to the appropriate UDM fields. Once activated, its mappings are merged into the UDM record, making the DNS query name and product event type available to detections.

**Learn more:** [Develop parser extensions | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/using-parser-extensions) · [Manage prebuilt parsers | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/manage-parser-updates)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a security engineer at a managed security service provider (MSSP) that is onboarding to Google Security Operations (SecOps). You must ensure that cases for every customer remain logically separated. How should you configure this logical segregation?

options.text: In Google SecOps SOAR settings, create a new environment for each customer.
In Google SecOps SOAR settings, create a role for each customer.
In Google SecOps SOAR settings, create a permissions group for each customer.
In Google SecOps Playbooks, create a playbook for each customer.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps SOAR environments provide logical data segregation. For MSSPs, an environment can represent a separate customer, isolating that customer's cases and related information from other environments.

**Learn more:** [Environments overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/admin-tasks/environments/work-with-environments) · [Get started with Google Security Operations SOAR](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/overview-and-introduction/getting-started-with-chronicle-soar)

options.text: Implement Assured Workloads by creating a folder for the business unit and assigning the relevant control package.

You are reviewing the security analyst team's playbook-action process. At present, security analysts go to the Playbooks tab in Google Security Operations (SecOps) for every alert and manually run steps assigned to a user.  
  
You need to show all actions from alerts awaiting user input in a single location for the analyst to execute. What should you do?

options.text: Enable approval links in the manual action and display them as clickable links to the user in a HTML widget in the Default Case View tab.
Add a general insight in your playbook to display manual action details to the user.
Use the Pending Actions widget in the Default Case View in settings.
Create an Alert View with the playbook that incorporates the Pending Actions widget.

questions.explanation:
The Pending Actions widget lists playbook actions that require analyst input to continue running. Configuring it in the Default Case View presents pending manual actions in the case overview, giving analysts a consolidated location to act on them.

**Learn more:** [Configure the default case view | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/investigate/working-with-cases/define-default-view-for-cases-admin) · [Manage playbook actions | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-actions-in-playbooks)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have been tasked with developing a new response process in a playbook to contain an endpoint. The new process must take the following actions:  
  
- Send an email to users who do not have a Google Security Operations (SecOps) account to request approval for endpoint containment.  
- Automatically continue executing its logic after the user responds.  
  
You plan to implement this process in the playbook using the Gmail integration. You want to minimize the effort required from the SOC analyst. What should you do?

options.text: Set the containment action to 'Manual' and assign the action to the user to execute or skip the containment action.
Set the containment action to 'Manual' and assign the action to the appropriate tier. Contact the user by email to request approval. The analyst chooses to execute or skip the containment action.
Use the 'Send Email' action to send an email requesting approval to contain the endpoint, and use the 'Wait For Thread Reply' action to receive the result. The analyst manually contains the endpoint.

Generate an approval link for the containment action and include the placeholder in the body of the 'Send Email' action. Configure additional playbook logic to manage approved or denied containment actions.

questions.explanation:
Google SecOps approval links let users outside the platform approve or decline a pending manual action through links included in an email. A containment action can be set to Manual with its approval-link placeholders inserted into a preceding Gmail Send Email action. Playbook logic can then branch or continue based on the approval or denial, without requiring an analyst to manually process the email response or carry out the decision.

**Learn more:** [Assign approval links in actions | Google Security Operations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/assign-approval-links-in-actions)
